subject: Blood Bank
q: A 2-year-old is newly diagnosed with beta-thalassaemia major and is about to receive his first transfusion. Which is the most appropriate blood product and pre-transfusion practice?
opts: Fresh whole blood, ABO and RhD compatible
Leucodepleted packed red cells, with extended Rh (C, c, E, e) and Kell phenotyping done before the first transfusion
Routinely washed packed red cells for every transfusion
Gamma-irradiated packed red cells from a first-degree relative for every transfusion
why: Whole blood delivers unnecessary plasma volume and leucocytes; packed cells are the standard for chronic transfusion
Correct: leucodepleted PRBC 10-15 mL/kg over 3-4 hours every 2-4 weeks, with extended Rh and Kell phenotyping BEFORE the first transfusion to prevent later alloimmunisation
Washing is reserved for repeated severe allergic reactions or IgA deficiency, not routine use
Relative-donor units risk transfusion-associated GVHD and HLA sensitisation before transplant, and are what routine practice avoids
exp: Chronic transfusion in thalassaemia major means leucodepleted packed red cells 10-15 mL/kg over 3-4 hours every 2-4 weeks, maintaining pre-transfusion haemoglobin at 9-10.5 g/dL. Leucoreduction prevents febrile non-haemolytic reactions, HLA alloimmunisation and CMV transmission. The commonly missed step is extended Rh (C, c, E, e) and Kell phenotyping BEFORE the first transfusion - skip it and alloimmunisation later makes cross-matching nearly impossible.

subject: Blood Bank
q: A 12-year-old with thalassaemia major who has received more than 40 transfusions presents 8 days after his last transfusion with low-grade fever, jaundice and a fall in haemoglobin from 10.4 to 7.1 g/dL. Indirect bilirubin and LDH are raised, the direct antiglobulin test is positive, and the antibody screen - negative three months ago - now shows anti-E. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Acute intravascular haemolytic reaction from ABO-incompatible transfusion
why: An acute ABO-incompatible reaction begins within minutes of starting the transfusion, with fever, loin pain and haemoglobinuria, not on day 8
TA-GVHD appears 1-6 weeks later with rash, diarrhoea, pancytopenia and deranged liver function, and the antiglobulin test is not the clue
Correct: haemolysis 3-14 days after transfusion with a positive DAT and a NEWLY detectable alloantibody is a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction from a secondary immune response
Hypersplenism causes a gradual fall in counts with a negative direct antiglobulin test and no new alloantibody
exp: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction occurs 3-14 days after transfusion: falling haemoglobin, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, raised LDH, positive direct antiglobulin test, and a newly detectable alloantibody (Rh antibodies and Kidd/Jka are commonest) from a secondary immune response. Separate it from acute ABO haemolysis (minutes, loin pain, haemoglobinuria) and TA-GVHD (1-6 weeks, rash, diarrhoea, pancytopenia). Prevention is extended red cell phenotype matching before chronic transfusion begins.
